newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Scoop up Nordics before troubles brew.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Scoop up Nordics before troubles brew.

text.p: Nordic bonds can outperform heavyweight European markets in the short term but economic fundamentals and concerns over the single European currency will crimp gains by the end of the year, analysts said on Thursday.

Both Finland and Sweden will gain on short term optimism towards European and Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) but Denmark should be the choice for investors unwilling to bank on EMU starting in Janaury 1999.

"I hold a quite a favourable short-term outlook for Swedish bonds," James MacKay, economist at PaineWebber in London, said. "All the high yielding markets are prone to deterioration in terms of the second and third quarters."
MacKay forecast the Sweden/Germany 10-year yield spread to squeeze to 100 basis points on a three month view from 150 basis points now.

Public disapproval has made Sweden a less likely candidate for EMU in the first round. Indeed, Finance Minister Erik Asbrink was set to announce before the end of May -- possibly on the May 1 holiday -- that Sweden was not yet ready for a single currency.
But that should not hold the market back, MacKay said.
"If anyone is unaware of that position now, they've had their eyes and ears shut," he said. "It clearly is a little bit of bad news for the long term prospects but it's largely factored in," he said.
He said the market would instead focus on falling inflation and if not further interst rate cuts, at least no rate rises for some time.
The European Union summit in Amsterdam in June should also give a boost as governments renew their commitment to EMU starting on time.
Further into the year those positives were more likely to become negatives, he added. All markets were also likely to be unsettled by the prospect of rising interest rates in Germany.

Stephanie Pfeifer, European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London, would avoid Sweden as elections approached next year and the temptation for the government to introduce stimulus measures to cut unemployment increased.
Instead, she would pick Finland, already strongly committed to EMU.

"For a long time there wasn't really any debate about EMU in Finland but it's really starting now and that is why we're starting to see some uncertainty. Longer term I think they will be in the first round," she said.
She expected the Finnish/Bund gap to slim to 40 basis in three months, 30 in six months and to 20 in 12 months. The spread is currently around 45 basis points.

"Inflation is still low and the outlook for rates is still quite positive," Pfeifer said. "It is growing very strongly but they have lots of spare capacity and there should not be much inflation pressure."
Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Securities Europe in London, would start pulling out of Sweden and opt for Finland or Denmark instead.

"I think we're coming to the end of an optimistic period about monetary union and the next move is going to be a deterioration in sentiment when markets realise how much economies like Germany are struggling," he said.
Both Finland and Denmark were buys on their fundamental merits, Jessop said.

"If nobody had thought of monetary union in the first place then you would probably still want to be a buyer of Denmark," he said, noting 10-year Denmark yields are 110 basis points below those in Britain.
--Jacqueline Thorpe, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176
